extraction_notes.note: The Positivity step cites 'the previous theorem' for $||b-a|| \le d_U(a,b)$, but in this source that result is Theorem 4, stated later; the edge TP4 -> PSP16 resolves the phrase by content.
Polygonal line and interval/polygonal-line length are textbook notions restated without citation, so marked external standard (uncited); d_U and the proved results are kept as paper.

nodes.name: Polygonal line
nodes.statement: Let $(E, \, ||\cdot||)$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with subset $A \subseteq E$. A \emph{polygonal line} in $A$ is a sequence of $n + 2$ points $u_{0}, \dots, u_{n+1}$ in $E$, such that each line segment connecting neighbouring vertices lies completely in $A$, i.e. \[ t \cdot u_{i} + (1 - t) \cdot u_{i + 1} \in A \quad \forall \, i = 0, \ldots, n \text{ and } t \in [0,\, 1]. \]
differentia: each line segment connecting neighbouring vertices lies completely in $A$
nodes.statement_short: A polygonal line in $A$ is a finite sequence of points whose consecutive segments all lie in $A$.
nodes.label: def:polygonalLine

nodes.name: Composition of polygonal lines
nodes.statement: Let $U$ be a subset of a normed vector space. Given a polygonal line in U, joining $x \in U$ and $y \in U$, together with another polygonal line joining $y$ and $z \in U$, then by connecting the two polygonal lines head-to-tail, the result is a polygonal line in U, joining $x$ and $z$.
assumptions: $U$ be a subset of a normed vector space
a polygonal line in U, joining $x \in U$ and $y \in U$, together with another polygonal line joining $y$ and $z \in U$
conclusions: by connecting the two polygonal lines head-to-tail, the result is a polygonal line in U, joining $x$ and $z$
nodes.label: lem:composition_of_polygonal_line

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: The construction of the composition of polygonal lines follows common sense: For the polygonal lines $a$, defined by $(x,\, a_1,\, \dots,\, a_n,\,y)$, and $b$, defined by $(y,\, b_1,\, \dots,\, b_m,\, z)$, we define the composition $a \circ b$ by the sequence $(x,\,a_1,\,\dots,\, a_n,\,y,\,b_1,\,\dots,\,b_m,\,z)$. It remains to show that each segment is still contained in $U$. This is trivial as the first $n + 2$ vertices belong to $a$ and are all contained in $U$. Similarly, the last $m + 2$ vertices belong to $b$, and are all contained in $U$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate the vertex sequences; each segment lies in one of the two original lines, hence in $U$.

nodes.name: Define the composition
nodes.statement: The construction of the composition of polygonal lines follows common sense: For the polygonal lines $a$, defined by $(x,\, a_1,\, \dots,\, a_n,\,y)$, and $b$, defined by $(y,\, b_1,\, \dots,\, b_m,\, z)$, we define the composition $a \circ b$ by the sequence $(x,\,a_1,\,\dots,\, a_n,\,y,\,b_1,\,\dots,\,b_m,\,z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $a \circ b$ by concatenating vertex sequences.

nodes.name: Segments stay in U
nodes.statement: It remains to show that each segment is still contained in $U$. This is trivial as the first $n + 2$ vertices belong to $a$ and are all contained in $U$. Similarly, the last $m + 2$ vertices belong to $b$, and are all contained in $U$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Each segment comes from $a$ or from $b$, so lies in $U$.

nodes.name: Existence of polygonal line in open connected set
nodes.statement: if $U$ is an open connected set of a normed vector space, then any two points of $U$ can be joined by a polygonal line in $U$.
assumptions: $U$ is an open connected set of a normed vector space
conclusions: any two points of $U$ can be joined by a polygonal line in $U$
nodes.label: thm:existence_of_polygonal_line

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: The case where $U = \emptyset$ is trivial. So we assume $U$ to be non-empty. Fix a point $x \in U$, and consider the set \[V \coloneqq \{u \in U \mid \exists \text{ a polygonal line connecting } x \text{ and } u.\}\] We want to show that $U = V$. To show that, we prove that $V$ is both closed and open in $U$ and $V$ is non-empty. The latter is true, as $x$ must be in $V$. For closedness, we show that $V = \bar{V}$, the closure of $V$. Fix a point $a \in \bar{V}$, then $\exists\, \epsilon > 0$, such that $B_{\epsilon}(a)\,\cap\,V \neq \emptyset$. Take a point $b \in B_{\epsilon}(a)\,\cap\,V$. Since $b \in V$, there is a polygonal line joining $x$ and $b$. Since $b \in B_{\epsilon}(a)$, there is a line segment joining $b$ and $a$, which is a polygonal line as well. By composing the two polygonal lines, we create a polygonal line joining $x$ and $a$. Hence $a \in V$. For openness, fix a point $a \in V$. We take an open ball centred at $a$ and contained in $U$, as $U$ is open. It can be shown that this open ball is contained in $V$ as well. It suffices to show that every point $b$ in the open ball can be connected to $x$ using a polygonal line, which can be constructed by composing the polygonal line joining $x$ and $a$ with the line segment joining $a$ and $b$. Since $V$ is both open and closed in $U$, it is either equal to $U$ or is the empty set. Since it is non-empty, we must have $U = V$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the set $V$ of points reachable from $x$ by polygonal lines is non-empty, open and closed in connected $U$, hence equals $U$.

nodes.name: Reduce to non-empty U
nodes.statement: The case where $U = \emptyset$ is trivial. So we assume $U$ to be non-empty.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $U$ is non-empty.

nodes.name: Define reachable set V
nodes.statement: Fix a point $x \in U$, and consider the set \[V \coloneqq \{u \in U \mid \exists \text{ a polygonal line connecting } x \text{ and } u.\}\]
nodes.statement_short: Let $V$ be the set of points joined to $x$ by a polygonal line.

nodes.name: Reduce to clopen and non-empty
nodes.statement: We want to show that $U = V$. To show that, we prove that $V$ is both closed and open in $U$ and $V$ is non-empty. The latter is true, as $x$ must be in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: $V$ is clopen in $U$ and non-empty ($x\in V$).

nodes.name: V is closed
nodes.statement: For closedness, we show that $V = \bar{V}$, the closure of $V$. Fix a point $a \in \bar{V}$, then $\exists\, \epsilon > 0$, such that $B_{\epsilon}(a)\,\cap\,V \neq \emptyset$. Take a point $b \in B_{\epsilon}(a)\,\cap\,V$. Since $b \in V$, there is a polygonal line joining $x$ and $b$. Since $b \in B_{\epsilon}(a)$, there is a line segment joining $b$ and $a$, which is a polygonal line as well. By composing the two polygonal lines, we create a polygonal line joining $x$ and $a$. Hence $a \in V$.
nodes.statement_short: Closure points of $V$ are reachable via a nearby point of $V$.

nodes.name: Closedness goal
nodes.statement: For closedness, we show that $V = \bar{V}$, the closure of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $V = \bar V$.

nodes.name: Pick a and nearby b
nodes.statement: Fix a point $a \in \bar{V}$, then $\exists\, \epsilon > 0$, such that $B_{\epsilon}(a)\,\cap\,V \neq \emptyset$. Take a point $b \in B_{\epsilon}(a)\,\cap\,V$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $a \in \bar V$ and $b \in V$ in a ball around $a$.

nodes.name: Two polygonal lines
nodes.statement: Since $b \in V$, there is a polygonal line joining $x$ and $b$. Since $b \in B_{\epsilon}(a)$, there is a line segment joining $b$ and $a$, which is a polygonal line as well.
nodes.statement_short: Get lines $x \to b$ and segment $b \to a$.

nodes.name: Compose to reach a
nodes.statement: By composing the two polygonal lines, we create a polygonal line joining $x$ and $a$. Hence $a \in V$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose them (Lemma 1) so $a \in V$.

nodes.name: V is open
nodes.statement: For openness, fix a point $a \in V$. We take an open ball centred at $a$ and contained in $U$, as $U$ is open. It can be shown that this open ball is contained in $V$ as well. It suffices to show that every point $b$ in the open ball can be connected to $x$ using a polygonal line, which can be constructed by composing the polygonal line joining $x$ and $a$ with the line segment joining $a$ and $b$.
nodes.statement_short: A ball around $a\in V$ in $U$ lies in $V$ by composing with segments.

nodes.name: Take a ball around a
nodes.statement: For openness, fix a point $a \in V$. We take an open ball centred at $a$ and contained in $U$, as $U$ is open.
nodes.statement_short: Take an open ball at $a$ inside $U$.

nodes.name: Ball lies in V
nodes.statement: It can be shown that this open ball is contained in $V$ as well. It suffices to show that every point $b$ in the open ball can be connected to $x$ using a polygonal line, which can be constructed by composing the polygonal line joining $x$ and $a$ with the line segment joining $a$ and $b$.
nodes.statement_short: Each ball point joins $x$ by composing with a segment.

nodes.name: Conclude U = V
nodes.statement: Since $V$ is both open and closed in $U$, it is either equal to $U$ or is the empty set. Since it is non-empty, we must have $U = V$.
nodes.statement_short: Clopen and non-empty in connected $U$ gives $V = U$.

nodes.name: Polygonal distance d_U
nodes.statement: Let $U$ be an open connected set of a Banach space $E$. For $a, b \in U$, we define $d_U(a,b)$ to be the infimum of the lengths of the polygonal lines contained in $U$ joining $a$ and $b$.
nodes.statement_short: $d_U(a,b)$ is the infimum of lengths of polygonal lines in $U$ from $a$ to $b$.
nodes.label: def:distance_in_U

nodes.name: d_U is a distance
nodes.statement: $d_U(a,b)$ is a distance in the topological space $U$.
assumptions: $U$ be an open connected set of a Banach space $E$
conclusions: \label{thm:d_U_is_a_distance} $d_U(a,b)$ is a distance in the topological space $U$.
nodes.label: thm:d_U_is_a_distance

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ be an arbitrary polygonal line joining $a$ to $b$ in $U$, defined by the sequence $a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n + 1}$, with $a_0 = a$ and $a_{n + 1} = b$ \textit{Positivity}: The length of $\varphi$ is $\text{Length}(\varphi) := \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_{i + 1} - a_i||$, which by the definition of a norm function is strictly non-negative. Since $d_U(a,b)$ is the infimum of a strictly non-negative set, it must itself be non-negative. If $d_U(a,b) = 0$, by the previous theorem we have $||b - a|| \leq d_U(a,b) = 0$, which implies $a = b$. \textit{Symmetry}: For any polygonal line $\varphi$ from $a$ to $b$ in $U$, the reverse line $\psi$ defined by $a_{n+1},\, \dots,\, a_0$ is a polygonal line from $b$ to $a$. $\text{Length}(\psi) = \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_i - a_{i + 1}|| = \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| = \text{Length}(\varphi)$, so the set of lengths of polygonal lines from $a$ to $b$ and from $b$ to $a$ are equivalent and therefore $d_U(a,b) = d_U(b,a)$. \textit{Triangle Inequality}: Let $\varphi$ be a polygonal line from $a$ to $b$ and $\psi$ be a polygonal line from $b$ to $c$. The composition of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ is a polygonal line $\theta$ from $a$ to $c$, where \[ \begin{cases} \varphi \text{ is defined by } (a, a_1, \dots, a_n, b) \\ \psi \text{ is defined by } (b, b_1, \dots, b_m, c)\\ \theta \text{ is defined by } (a, a_1, \dots, a_n, b, b_1, \dots, b_m, c) \end{cases} \] By the definition of infimum, $d_U(a,c) = \inf \text{Length}(\theta) \leq \text{Length}(\theta) = \text{Length}(\varphi) + \text{Length}(\psi)$. Since $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are arbitrary, we take the infimum on the right hand side, and hence $d_U(a,c) \leq d_U(a,b) + d_U(b,c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Check positivity, symmetry (reverse lines) and triangle inequality (compose lines, take infimum).

nodes.name: Fix a polygonal line
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ be an arbitrary polygonal line joining $a$ to $b$ in $U$, defined by the sequence $a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n + 1}$, with $a_0 = a$ and $a_{n + 1} = b$
nodes.statement_short: Fix an arbitrary polygonal line $\varphi$ from $a$ to $b$.

nodes.name: Positivity
nodes.statement: \textit{Positivity}: The length of $\varphi$ is $\text{Length}(\varphi) := \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_{i + 1} - a_i||$, which by the definition of a norm function is strictly non-negative. Since $d_U(a,b)$ is the infimum of a strictly non-negative set, it must itself be non-negative. If $d_U(a,b) = 0$, by the previous theorem we have $||b - a|| \leq d_U(a,b) = 0$, which implies $a = b$.
nodes.statement_short: Lengths are non-negative, and $d_U=0$ forces $a=b$ via $\|b-a\|\le d_U$.

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: \textit{Symmetry}: For any polygonal line $\varphi$ from $a$ to $b$ in $U$, the reverse line $\psi$ defined by $a_{n+1},\, \dots,\, a_0$ is a polygonal line from $b$ to $a$. $\text{Length}(\psi) = \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_i - a_{i + 1}|| = \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| = \text{Length}(\varphi)$, so the set of lengths of polygonal lines from $a$ to $b$ and from $b$ to $a$ are equivalent and therefore $d_U(a,b) = d_U(b,a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reversing a line preserves its length.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: \textit{Triangle Inequality}: Let $\varphi$ be a polygonal line from $a$ to $b$ and $\psi$ be a polygonal line from $b$ to $c$. The composition of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ is a polygonal line $\theta$ from $a$ to $c$, where \[ \begin{cases} \varphi \text{ is defined by } (a, a_1, \dots, a_n, b) \\ \psi \text{ is defined by } (b, b_1, \dots, b_m, c)\\ \theta \text{ is defined by } (a, a_1, \dots, a_n, b, b_1, \dots, b_m, c) \end{cases} \] By the definition of infimum, $d_U(a,c) = \inf \text{Length}(\theta) \leq \text{Length}(\theta) = \text{Length}(\varphi) + \text{Length}(\psi)$. Since $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are arbitrary, we take the infimum on the right hand side, and hence $d_U(a,c) \leq d_U(a,b) + d_U(b,c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose lines and take infima.

nodes.name: Mean Value Theorem in a connected open set
nodes.statement: Let $U$ be a connected open set of a Banach space $E$. Let $f: U \rightarrow F$ be a differentiable mapping with values in a Banach space $F$. Assume that \[ ||f'(x)|| \leq k \quad \forall x \in U \] then for any $x_1,x_2 \in U$, $||f(x_1)-f(x_2)|| \leq k \cdot d_U(x_1,x_2)$.
assumptions: $U$ be a connected open set of a Banach space $E$
$f: U \rightarrow F$ be a differentiable mapping with values in a Banach space $F$
nodes.statement_short: A differentiable map with $\|f'\|\le k$ on connected open $U$ is $k$-Lipschitz for the polygonal distance $d_U$.
nodes.label: thm:mean_value_theorem_in_connected_open_set

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Let $x_1,x_2 \in U$ and $l$ a polygonal line contained in $U$ joining $x_1$ and $x_2$. Suppose $l$ is defined by $n + 1$ vertices $a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n+1}$, where $a_0=x_1, a_{n+1} = x_2$ and $a_i \in U$. Then from the mean value inequality on each interval $(a_i, a_{i+1})$, we have $||f(a_i)-f(a_{i+1})|| \leq k \cdot ||a_i-a_{i+1}||$. From the triangle inequality we have \begin{align*} ||f(x_1)-f(x_2)|| &\leq \sum_{i=0}^{n} ||f(a_i)-f(a_{i+1})|| \\ &\leq \sum_{i=0}^{n} k \cdot ||a_i-a_{i+1}||\\ &= k \cdot \text{Length}(l) \end{align*} as $\text{Length}(l)$ is the sum of the length of each interval. Therefore, taking the infimum we get \[ ||f(x_1)-f(x_2)|| \leq k \cdot \inf{\text{Length}(l)} = k\cdot d_U(x_1,x_2) \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the mean value inequality on each segment of a polygonal line, sum by the triangle inequality, take the infimum over lines.

nodes.name: Fix a polygonal line
nodes.statement: Let $x_1,x_2 \in U$ and $l$ a polygonal line contained in $U$ joining $x_1$ and $x_2$. Suppose $l$ is defined by $n + 1$ vertices $a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n+1}$, where $a_0=x_1, a_{n+1} = x_2$ and $a_i \in U$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a polygonal line $l$ from $x_1$ to $x_2$ with vertices $a_i$.

nodes.name: Mean value inequality per segment
nodes.statement: Then from the mean value inequality on each interval $(a_i, a_{i+1})$, we have $||f(a_i)-f(a_{i+1})|| \leq k \cdot ||a_i-a_{i+1}||$.
nodes.statement_short: Segment-wise mean value inequality.

nodes.name: Sum over segments
nodes.statement: From the triangle inequality we have \begin{align*} ||f(x_1)-f(x_2)|| &\leq \sum_{i=0}^{n} ||f(a_i)-f(a_{i+1})|| \\ &\leq \sum_{i=0}^{n} k \cdot ||a_i-a_{i+1}||\\ &= k \cdot \text{Length}(l) \end{align*} as $\text{Length}(l)$ is the sum of the length of each interval.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality gives bound $k\cdot$Length$(l)$.

nodes.name: Take infimum
nodes.statement: Therefore, taking the infimum we get \[ ||f(x_1)-f(x_2)|| \leq k \cdot \inf{\text{Length}(l)} = k\cdot d_U(x_1,x_2) \]
nodes.statement_short: Infimum over $l$ gives $k\,d_U$.

nodes.name: Length of an interval
nodes.statement: Let $(E, ||\cdot||)$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb{R}$. The \emph{length of an interval} with origin $a \in E$ and end $b \in E$ is $d(a,b) := ||b - a||$.
nodes.statement_short: The length of the interval from $a$ to $b$ is $\|b-a\|$.
nodes.label: def:intervalLength

nodes.name: Length of a polygonal line
nodes.statement: Given a polygonal line $\varphi$ defined by $(a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n+1})$, with some fixed $n \geq 0$ the \emph{length of the polygonal line} $\varphi$ is the sum of the lengths of the intervals from which it is formed: \[ \text{Length}(\varphi) := \sum_{i=0}^{n} d(a_i, a_{i+1}) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} || a_{i+1} - a_i || \]
nodes.genus: sum of the lengths of the intervals from which it is formed
nodes.statement_short: Length of a polygonal line is the sum of its segment lengths.
nodes.label: def:polygonalLineLength

nodes.name: Norm of sum of differences bound (generalized triangle inequality)
nodes.statement: Given a sequence $(a_i)_{i=0}^{n}$ with $a_i \in E$ for some $n \geq 1$, $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \geq ||a_n - a_0||$
assumptions: a sequence $(a_i)_{i=0}^{n}$ with $a_i \in E$ for some $n \geq 1$
nodes.label: lemma:norm_sum_at_least_sum_norm

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Base Case ($n=1$):} For $n=1$, we need $||a_1 - a_0|| \geq ||a_1 - a_0||$ which follows immediately by reflexivity. \item \textbf{Induction Hypothesis:} Assume that the result holds for any such sequence $(b_i)_{i=0}^k$. That is, \[ \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}||b_{i+1} - b_i|| \geq ||b_k - b_0|| \] \item \textbf{Induction Step:} We want to show that $\sum_{i=0}^{k}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \geq ||a_{k+1} - a_0||$ follows from this assumption. For some arbitrary sequence $(a_i)_{i=0}^{k+1}$, \begin{align*} ||a_{k+1} - a_0|| &= ||(a_{k+1} - a_k) + (a_k - a_0)|| \\ &\leq ||a_{k+1} - a_k|| + ||a_k - a_0|| \\ &\leq ||a_{k+1} - a_k|| + \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \\ &= \sum_{i=0}^{k}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \end{align*} \end{itemize} Therefore, by the principle of mathematical induction, $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \geq ||a_n - a_0||$ for any such sequence with any $n \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$; the inductive step splits off the last difference with the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: \textbf{Base Case ($n=1$):} For $n=1$, we need $||a_1 - a_0|| \geq ||a_1 - a_0||$ which follows immediately by reflexivity.
nodes.statement_short: $n=1$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: \textbf{Induction Hypothesis:} Assume that the result holds for any such sequence $(b_i)_{i=0}^k$. That is, \[ \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}||b_{i+1} - b_i|| \geq ||b_k - b_0|| \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume the bound for length-$k$ sequences.

nodes.name: Induction step
nodes.statement: \textbf{Induction Step:} We want to show that $\sum_{i=0}^{k}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \geq ||a_{k+1} - a_0||$ follows from this assumption. For some arbitrary sequence $(a_i)_{i=0}^{k+1}$, \begin{align*} ||a_{k+1} - a_0|| &= ||(a_{k+1} - a_k) + (a_k - a_0)|| \\ &\leq ||a_{k+1} - a_k|| + ||a_k - a_0|| \\ &\leq ||a_{k+1} - a_k|| + \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \\ &= \sum_{i=0}^{k}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality plus hypothesis.

nodes.name: Conclude by induction
nodes.statement: Therefore, by the principle of mathematical induction, $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \geq ||a_n - a_0||$ for any such sequence with any $n \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by induction.

nodes.name: Polygonal line length at least interval length
nodes.statement: The length of a polygonal line $\varphi$ defined by $a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n + 1}$ for some fixed $n \geq 0$ between origin $a = a_0$ and end $b = a_{n+1}$ is at least equal to the length of the interval between them: \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n}||a_{i+1} - a_i|| \geq ||b - a|| \]
assumptions: a polygonal line $\varphi$ defined by $a_0,\, \dots,\, a_{n + 1}$ for some fixed $n \geq 0$ between origin $a = a_0$ and end $b = a_{n+1}$
nodes.label: thm:polygonal_line_length_at_least_interval_length

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: The result follows immediately from the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Lemma 2.
